items.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Nat Cole. Peggy Lee. Sinatra. All those people. I mean I’ve worked in that studio which thank God they made into a landmark so they can’t tear it up, like most of them are gone.

ctx.x: I’m so glad you brought that up. I’m showing my age. But if I have the 60s channel on and I’m hearing any number of things, Dusty Springfield or anything, like there’s no straining to hear what she’s saying. Now if I turn on current music and you know, here we go, current music, but I’m always straining, even with maybe Tom Petty or those kind of people. What’s he saying. Like I’m listening hard. Is it your feeling that the music and the bass have come up and the vocal hasn’t come with it?

You’ve got to understand where it’s going now. It’s all compressed so much. It squashes all the music and the vocal. But Tom Petty at least recorded in real studios. Now it’s people who are trying to get in the business are doing it on their computers with all the plug-ins, where we had millions of dollars of equipment in the control room, now you can access a similar sound on the computer. But one of the things — I mean this goes back to the 40s with Sinatra and people. The vocal had to be here and the music had…

Even as a studio player, I always listened at a really low level to hear where the vocal was sitting. More so than everything else. Everything else we could kind of mix ourselves as musicians. But you had to make sure the vocal was just right — I always said I strived to make records that were transparent. That you could walk into the mix and it would surround you. And that’s gone. Because everything is so compressed now. There’s a few people that make records like that but we took our cue from those days — the…
